title: Kubernetes Networking, Pod Lifecycle, and Operations
description: Test your deep knowledge of Kubernetes cluster networking, CNI implementations, pod graceful shutdown sequences, and service routing mechanisms.

questions.text: Why do large Kubernetes clusters (thousands of services and pods) typically switch `kube-proxy` from `iptables` mode to `IPVS` mode?

options.text: IPVS enforces mutual TLS (mTLS) natively in kernel space without sidecar proxies
iptables evaluates routing rules linearly in O(n) time, whereas IPVS uses kernel hash tables providing O(1) packet lookup regardless of service count
iptables cannot support HTTP/2 and gRPC streams, while IPVS operates at Layer 7
IPVS eliminates the need for a CNI plugin by directly handling container network interfaces

questions.explanation: In clusters with tens of thousands of services, `iptables` rule evaluation degrades significantly because rules are organized as a sequential list ($O(n)$ packet traversal) and synchronized by re-generating the entire table. IPVS uses kernel IP set hash tables, offering $O(1)$ packet matching and negligible sync overhead under high churn.

questions.text: When a Kubernetes Pod is deleted, which sequence of events accurately describes the lifecycle of traffic termination and container shutdown?

options.text: The container receives SIGKILL immediately, then kube-proxy removes the IP from Service endpoints
Pod state becomes Terminating; endpoints controller asynchronously removes the Pod IP from endpoints while the container executes preStop hooks and receives SIGTERM concurrently
All active TCP connections are severed by the Linux kernel, then kubelet sends SIGTERM
kubelet waits until all inbound HTTP requests return status 200 before sending SIGTERM

questions.explanation: Pod deletion triggers two parallel workflows: the Endpoints/EndpointSlice controller detects deletion and propagates IP removal to kube-proxy/ingress, while kubelet executes the container's `preStop` hook and sends SIGTERM. Because endpoint propagation takes several seconds, applications typically add a short preStop sleep (e.g. 5-10s) to avoid receiving new connections after SIGTERM.

questions.text: What is the primary operational characteristic and use case of a Kubernetes 'Headless Service' (`clusterIP: None`)?

options.text: It bypasses kube-proxy VIP allocation; DNS queries for the service name return direct A/AAAA/SRV records for individual matching Pod IPs, enabling peer discovery for stateful distributed databases
It exposes pods directly to the public internet without an ingress controller or cloud load balancer
It prevents pods from making outbound internet requests to ensure PCI-DSS compliance
It runs the pod directly on the host network namespace without a container veth pair

questions.explanation: Headless services do not allocate a ClusterIP virtual IP and do not perform load balancing via kube-proxy. CoreDNS returns the set of actual Pod IPs associated with the selector, allowing stateful systems (e.g., Kafka, Cassandra, ZooKeeper) to directly discover and communicate with specific peers.

questions.text: What is the key performance trade-off between an overlay CNI (e.g., Flannel/Calico with VXLAN) and a cloud-native flat routed CNI (e.g., AWS VPC CNI, GKE Alias IPs)?

options.text: Overlay networks have zero MTU overhead, whereas flat networks encapsulate every packet in UDP

Overlay networks wrap inner packet headers with outer UDP/VXLAN headers causing MTU reduction and CPU encapsulation cost; flat routed networks assign native VPC IPs to Pods, avoiding encapsulation at the cost of IP address exhaustion
Flat networks cannot use NetworkPolicies, while overlay networks can only run in single-zone clusters
Overlay networks require dedicated hardware ASICs on every worker node

questions.explanation: Overlay networks encapsulate container traffic in VXLAN/Geneve UDP packets across nodes, adding ~50 bytes per packet and minor CPU overhead. Flat VPC CNIs assign real VPC subnet IPs directly to container interfaces, providing line-rate wire speed and native cloud routing, but can quickly exhaust VPC subnet IP quotas.

questions.text: Which architectural limitation of the traditional Kubernetes `Ingress` resource does the Kubernetes `Gateway API` resolve?

options.text: Ingress could only route HTTP traffic on port 80, whereas Gateway API only supports gRPC

Ingress is a monolithic resource that blends infrastructure provisioning and application routing, causing vendor-specific annotation sprawl; Gateway API splits concerns across GatewayClass (infra), Gateway (cluster ops), and HTTPRoute (app developer)
Ingress required recompiling the Linux kernel for each new routing rule
Gateway API removes the need for Envoy or NGINX proxies completely

questions.explanation: The traditional `Ingress` resource forced cluster operators and application developers into a single shared resource with non-standard vendor annotations (e.g., `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/*`). Gateway API provides role-oriented, expressive CRDs (`GatewayClass`, `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`, `GRPCRoute`) with standardized multi-tenant support.
